data.title: 3 online sales factors to watch in 2026 holiday shopping forecasts
data.description:
Online retailers preparing for the 2026 holiday shopping season are about to face a wave of customers unlike any they have seen in previous years, as forecasts call for ecommerce sales to grow at a rate similar to 2025.

The Cyber 5, a period which includes Thanksgiving Day, Black Friday and the three days that follow, begins on Nov. 26 in 2026, concluding on Cyber Monday, which falls on Nov. 30. Over those days, artificial intelligence (AI) and agentic commerce will be put to use through new offerings for shoppers from Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta and other providers, which are trying to command larger roles in research, payments and more. Meanwhile, online retailers will put their own new tools to the test, as they cater to a rising share of AI-associated traffic referrals and AI agents that are browsing their ecommerce sites on behalf of human users.

As consumers continue to face pressure from inflation, tariff-related costs and other macroeconomic factors, online shoppers care about how AI options such as Google’s Gemini and Meta’s Muse can help them compare prices and find deals. In fact, 26% of online shoppers surveyed in October by Digital Commerce 360 and Bizrate Insights said that this was their primary reason for using AI when buying products.

In the meantime, retailers’ ecommerce sites, ChatGPT apps and optimization strategies for content and catalog data will all play roles in their pursuit of traffic and conversion that helps them to meet their year-end sales targets.

Sales projections for the 2026 holiday shopping season

Adobe’s forecast for the final two months of 2026 calls for online sales to grow 6.7% year over year to reach $275.1 billion. That growth would be comparable to — but slightly down from — the 6.8% growth achieved in 2025 by Adobe’s own measurements.

A wider forecast from Deloitte, published in September, set expectations for total holiday retail sales (including ecommerce and physical stores) at $1.70 trillion to $1.71 trillion for activity in November 2026 through January 2027. Sales at that level would mean growth of 4.0 to 4.8% from a year earlier, after that year-ago period saw 4.1% year-over-year growth.

Meanwhile, November results published by ICSC (formerly the International Council of Shopping Centers) on Nov. 18 showed that 88% of 1,007 U.S. adults surveyed planned to shop at some point during the Cyber 5. The same report showed that 77% expected to spend the same or more than they did in 2025.

“Shoppers are increasingly willing to switch and/or try new brands in order to find the best value — making Thanksgiving Weekend a prime opportunity for retailers to earn their business,” said Tom McGee, president and CEO of ICSC. “With AI giving consumers more tools than ever to research products, compare prices, and find deals, shoppers are taking a more active role in deciding where their money goes.”

Increasing AI traffic conversion

Adobe projects that AI-associated referral traffic to online retailers’ websites will be up 159% on Thanksgiving, 95% on Black Friday and 88% on Cyber Monday from its previous levels in 2025. Those percentages are significantly smaller than the four-digit percentages of year-over-year growth seen during various periods in 2025. However, another key metric has been moving upward, according to Adobe analysts — and that is the conversion rate for AI-referred shoppers.

In August, Adobe Analytics shared that it has seen AI-referrals’ conversion rates outperform non-AI referrals for 11 consecutive months, with AI referrals generating 53% more revenue per visit than other shoppers. Then, in September, Adobe observed that difference to be 83% higher per visit when compared with non-AI traffic. That was the largest gap observed in 2026 and an inverted relationship from a year earlier. Essentially, Adobe saw AI-associated traffic go from being less effective, worth less than half the value of non-AI-referred visits, to being worth nearly twice as much.

Elsewhere, Salesforce predicted that AI agents would be responsible for 20% of all holiday ecommerce traffic in 2026, according to Caila Schwartz, director of consumer strategy and insights for Salesforce. Schwartz wrote in July that her company, which provides an ecommerce platform for retailers, expects to see 1 in 3 ecommerce sites using personal, site-specific agents to serve shoppers during the period it calls Cyber Week (the Tuesday before Thanksgiving and six days that follow) in 2026.

Discount levels and windows for online holiday discounts

Deep discounts for the season began as far back as October in 2026, with Amazon’s Prime Big Deal Days at the beginning of the month. Online shoppers spent $9.86 billion on Oct. 6 and 7, as that event played out, according to Adobe. Looking ahead, the company’s forecast assesses that discounts during the Cyber 5 (which Adobe refers to as Cyber Week) would reach up to 30% off listed prices.

Adobe anticipates that those discounts will hit 21% in the days immediately preceding Thanksgiving and then settle into 10% to 15% during December. Ultimately, those deals would be roughly in line with the levels seen for the 2025 holiday season.

“Sales and discounts (56%) are the most cited factors in shoppers’ decision-making around which retailers to shop throughout the holiday season,” wrote Lea Grgich, a senior research analyst at the National Retail Federation.

The industry group released its own survey results on October 28, showing that 64% of shoppers expected to wait until Thanksgiving to do most of their holiday shopping in 2026. That was up from 51% in 2020.

data.title: Tractor Supply joins Uber Marketplace, adding delivery options for rural customers
data.description:
Tractor Supply Co. is adding Uber as a delivery partner, making its products available through the Uber, Uber Eats and Postmates apps. The companies announced the nationwide partnership Nov. 12.

Customers can order pet food, animal care products, lawn and garden supplies, tools and outdoor gear for on-demand delivery. Tractor Supply operated 2,486 stores in 49 states as of Sept. 26, along with 135 Petsense by Tractor Supply stores. The announcement refers to Tractor Supply’s stores, not Petsense locations.

Tractor Supply is No. 83 in the Top 1000 Database. The database tracks North America’s largest online retailers, ranking them by annual ecommerce sales and more.

Tractor Supply expands delivery beyond metro areas

Uber’s pitch centers on geography. Tractor Supply stores are concentrated in rural, exurban and suburban communities, which Uber sees as an opportunity to extend on-demand delivery beyond major cities.

“The need for convenience doesn’t stop at the city limits,” said Nathan Bernheim, Uber’s head of retail partnerships, in the announcement.

Matthew Rubin, Tractor Supply’s senior vice president and president of digital and ecommerce, said the deal gives customers more ways to shop. It also introduces the retailer to “millions of Uber users” who may not have shopped there before, he said. “Tractor Supply is continually finding new ways to serve customers and make Life Out Here more convenient,” Rubin added.

Customers can search for Tractor Supply in the Uber, Uber Eats or Postmates app, or browse the Retail section. They then pick a store, build a cart, choose a delivery option and track the order in the app. 

To mark the launch, Uber is offering $20 off Tractor Supply orders of $60 or more. Fees and terms apply.

The announcement did not specify delivery speeds or fees.

Tractor Supply’s relationship with Instacart and DoorDash

Uber is the second delivery platform Tractor Supply added this year. In July, the retailer announced it had joined Instacart Marketplace, a competitor to Uber. 

At the time of the announcement, Tractor Supply and Instacart representatives shared similar sentiments about expanding same-day delivery to rural customers and introducing Tractor Supply to new shoppers.

Tractor Supply has also had a delivery partnership with DoorDash since 2022. Now the delivery market is consolidating. 

On Oct. 29, DoorDash announced that it would acquire Instacart in a deal valued at $17 billion. The deal needs regulatory and Instacart shareholder approval. The companies expect it to close near the end of 2027 or in the first half of 2028.

Until then, Instacart will operate independently. DoorDash expects to keep the Instacart brand, app and enterprise technology products afterward.

Tractor Supply’s own delivery network

The Uber deal builds on a store-based delivery network Tractor Supply has spent the past year and a half expanding. CEO Hal Lawton said in September that the retailer has offered delivery from stores for five or six years, including same-day and two- to three-day options. Its newer “Final Mile” system links every three to four stores in a hub-and-spoke arrangement, with one store serving four.

Tractor Supply completed as many last-mile deliveries in the first half of 2026 as it did in all of 2025, Lawton said. Delivery from stores led double-digit digital sales growth in fiscal Q2, even as comparable store sales fell 1.5% in a difficult quarter.

The retailer is also building out its supply chain. In September, Tractor Supply opened its 11th distribution center in Nampa, Idaho, an 865,000-square-foot facility that will support 123 stores across nine states in its first year. The center was designed to serve more than 200 stores at full capacity.

data.title: Asics uses AI-powered drones to recover misplaced inventory 60% faster
data.description:
Asics America Corp. is using autonomous drones to find misplaced merchandise at its primary North American distribution center, a move the company says is helping it curb the risk of unfulfilled orders.

The technology, developed by Corvus Robotics, is helping the sportswear brand recover misplaced inventory about 60% faster, according to a Nov. 10 announcement from the warehouse automation provider.

At Asics’ facility in Byhalia, Mississippi, drones now conduct inventory counts in two key storage areas every month, up from twice annually. The higher frequency lets Asics offer merchandise on online marketplaces that were previously withheld due to fulfillment concerns.

Asics America, based in Irvine, California, is the U.S. subsidiary of Japanese sportswear company Asics Corp.

How Asics uses drones to count warehouse inventory

Asics’ 855,000-square-foot distribution center in Byhalia houses nearly 3 million units of footwear, apparel and accessories across roughly 44,000 stock-keeping units.

The facility fulfills ecommerce orders while also supplying Asics stores and wholesale customers. All three channels draw from the same inventory pool, and customer returns are processed there as well.

Asics is using Corvus One drones in two warehouse zones: a singles area that stores returned merchandise and individual pairs of shoes, and a case reserve area that holds full cartons.

The drones perform seven scheduled flights a night, starting at around 7 p.m., Corvus said. Using onboard computer vision and spatial reasoning, they navigate aisles less than 6 feet wide without needing additional warehouse infrastructure, such as markers or beacons.

During each flight, the drones scan universal product codes while also counting boxes stored at each location. Corvus said the system compares those counts with barcode scans, identifying inventory discrepancies. The following morning, a warehouse employee reviews the results using images and video captured during the flights.

“Now we can just look at the footage and we can tell exactly what’s going on with it in the locations before we have to send someone out,” Angela Williford, inventory control operations manager at Asics America, said in a Corvus video case study. “If it’s something that we can correct from the desk, we’ll correct it then.”

More frequent counts help Asics recover merchandise

During one three-month period, drones identified 26 misplaced cases containing more than 200 pairs of shoes. Without the additional counts, those items could have remained unavailable for sale until the next scheduled inventory review, Asics said.

Koestler estimated that Asics is recovering misplaced inventory roughly 60% faster than before the deployment.

“You don’t want to have to count a thousand locations to find the four or five that have problems,” he said in the video case study.

The automation has also shifted how warehouse employees spend their time. Rather than focusing on routine cycle counts, workers can dedicate more effort to inventory reconciliation, discrepancy investigations and wholesale-support projects, according to the companies.

Corvus also said the drones reduce the need for lift equipment during inventory counts, limiting traffic in the facility’s narrow aisles.

Asics makes more inventory available to marketplaces

The inventory gains have also influenced how Asics sells products through online marketplaces.

Before adopting the drone system, Asics withheld between 12 and 15 units out of every 100 from the inventory feeds it provided to marketplace partners, according to Corvus. The company did so because products shown as available might be missing or difficult to locate when orders arrived.

With monthly counts providing greater visibility into stock levels, Asics said it now publishes its full inventory availability feed.

Corvus said the change allows Asics to offer more merchandise at full price rather than potentially liquidating it at a discount. The companies did not disclose how much additional revenue the change has generated.

Other retailers expand warehouse automation

Asics is among a growing number of companies deploying inventory drones to improve warehouse operations.

After deploying Corvus’ technology, health and wellness retailer GNC increased inventory counts at its distribution centers in Indianapolis and Phoenix, according to a case study. Counts rose to as many as 10 to 12 times per year, up from two to four.

Likewise, Southern Glazer’s Wine & Spirits expanded its drone deployment to nine distribution centers. The beverage distributor reported a 100-basis-point improvement in cases handled per hour, Corvus said.

Other major retailers are investing in different forms of warehouse automation. Walmart Inc. recently announced plans to expand Symbotic automation technology across 25 U.S. regional distribution centers. The retailer said the rollout is designed to support inventory management, increase storage capacity and improve product flow throughout its supply chain.

Walmart ranks No. 2 in Digital Commerce 360’s Top 1000 Database. The database tracks North America’s largest online retailers, ranking them by annual ecommerce sales and more.

data.title: Adobe data shows online holiday spending up 9.1% ahead of Thanksgiving
data.description:
As retailers prepare for Thanksgiving Day to kick off the Cyber 5, a five-day period that ends on Cyber Monday, new data from Adobe Analytics suggests that online shoppers have already spent more than $82.5 billion.

That total, which represents activity across 1 trillion visits to U.S. retail sites from Nov. 1 through Nov. 22, 2026, represents a 9.1% increase from the comparable period a year earlier. Moreover, those 22 days included two individual days where online shoppers spent at least $4 billion, the first time that has occurred in the weeks ahead of Thanksgiving and Black Friday, according to Adobe analysts.

Adobe also noted a rise in buy now, pay later (BNPL) use online, with associated purchases up 6.5% year over year to $6.1 billion.

The data comes as holiday shopping forecasts from Adobe, Salesforce and other sources anticipate new ecommerce records will be set in November and December as artificial intelligence (AI) drives rising conversion rates for shoppers using agentic commerce to research, discover and make purchases.

Pre-Thanksgiving holiday spending data in 2026

Online shoppers spent more than $3 billion each day during the 22 days covered in Adobe’s holiday spending data. For comparison, its analysts shared that only 21 of the comparable 22 days in 2025 included single-day spending above $3 billion.

If Adobe’s projections prove to be accurate, Cyber 5 sales alone will bring in $47.5 billion in online spending, up 7.4% from a year ago. That total would account for 17.3% of the full $275.1 billion that Adobe analysts expect to be spent from Nov. 1 to Dec. 31, 2026.

The same analysts predict that Cyber Monday will retain its status as the busiest online shopping day of the holiday season and full calendar year, with its single-day ecommerce sales growing 6.2% year over year to $15.1 billion.

Nevertheless, Adobe also projects that Black Friday and Thanksgiving single-day sales online will see even stronger growth. Its forecast calls for Black Friday online sales to increase 9.2% year over year to $12.9 billion and Thanksgiving ecommerce sales to grow 8.5% to $6.9 billion.

AI-driven traffic to ecommerce sites

So far during the 2026 holiday shopping season, Adobe has observed AI-referred visits to U.S. retailers’ ecommerce sites increase 127% year over year. During the Cyber 5, it expects year-over-year growth for the same metric to hit 110%. In addition, it projects that AI-associated traffic will be up 159% on Thanksgiving, 95% on Black Friday and 88% on Cyber Monday.

The company’s own survey of 1,000 U.S. consumers found that 81% felt AI improved their online shopping experiences. Meanwhile, 27% indicated that they used AI more often when shopping during sales events and holidays.

In its own holiday spending forecast, Salesforce projects that the Cyber Week period that it tracks, running from Nov. 24 through Nov. 30, will see $357 billion in global online sales. Notably, the customer relationship management (CRM) and ecommerce platform provider also expects to see $75.8 billion of that total influenced by AI tools, including AI agents. Already, Salesforce has observed AI-driven traffic to retailers’ websites rise 104% year over year.

data.title: Gap Q3 earnings: Online sales rise 3% as holiday outlook weakens
data.description:
Gap Inc.’s namesake brand continued its turnaround in fiscal Q3 2026, helping offset weaker performance elsewhere across its portfolio. Even so, the retailer lowered its full-year outlook after unseasonably warm weather slowed demand for fall apparel, executives said.

In its fiscal third quarter ended Oct. 31, Gap Inc. reported net sales of $4.01 billion, up 2% year over year. Online sales rose 3%, outpacing 1% growth in store sales. Ecommerce accounted for 40% of quarterly revenue, which was unchanged from a year earlier.

Performance varied widely across Gap Inc.’s four major brands. During Q3, its namesake Gap banner posted double-digit sales growth, while Old Navy’s comparable sales stabilized after declining in the prior quarter. Banana Republic reported a 3% year-over-year sales decline.

Athleta faced steeper declines in Q3 as Gap Inc. named Ashley Kechter the activewear brand’s next president and CEO and launched a broader review of the business.

Kechter, who will assume the role on Dec. 14, most recently served as global president of Vuori and previously held leadership roles across Gap Inc.’s portfolio, including Banana Republic, Old Navy and Gap.

“Ashley grew up in the company and understands our culture and what it takes to operate at scale,” CEO Richard Dickson said on the earnings call.

On a positive note, executives said sales trends have improved as temperatures cooled. Gap also expects lower-than-previously-assumed U.S. tariff rates to add roughly $46 million to operating profit this year.

Gap Inc. ranks No. 19 in Digital Commerce 360’s Top 2000 Database, which tracks North America’s largest online retailers by their annual ecommerce sales and more.

The company is also No. 577 in Digital Commerce 360 and ReFiBuy’s AI Commerce Rankings. That set of rankings is available in the Top 1000 Pro with AI Database.

Gap Inc. web sales by year

Vuori ranks No. 558 in the Top 2000 and No. 332 in the AI Commerce Rankings.

Gap brand continues turnaround

Gap Inc.’s comparable sales, which include ecommerce, were flat year over year in its fiscal Q3 2026. Adjusted earnings per share increased 32% to $0.82, according to the company’s earnings release.

Reported net income in Q3 rose to $311 million, up from $236 million a year earlier.

Across its banners, the namesake Gap brand posted the strongest gains. Net sales rose 11% year over year to $1.06 billion, driven by denim and fleece. Comparable sales rose 9%, marking the brand’s 12th consecutive quarter of growth, Dickson said.

Old Navy, Gap Inc.’s largest brand, also showed signs of improvement. Net sales increased 1% to $2.27 billion, accounting for more than half of the company’s quarterly revenue. Comparable sales were flat after declining 4% in Q2.

Dickson credited stronger fall assortments — particularly denim, activewear and knits — along with more focused marketing and pricing changes aimed at improving value for shoppers.

In November, Michael Francis assumed the role of Old Navy president and CEO after serving as the brand’s chief customer officer.

“His deep engagement and stewardship over the past several months, particularly across marketing and merchandising, has been impactful in Q3,” Dickson said.

Banana Republic, Athleta face challenges

Banana Republic, meanwhile, reported a 3% decline in both net sales and comparable sales in Q3. Dickson attributed the weakness in part to softer demand for women’s apparel.

“First, the assortment was overweighted towards cold weather categories, including sweaters and outerwear, amid warmer-than-expected temperatures, particularly in October,” he said. “Second, we didn’t get the fashion and color point of view right in parts of the women’s assortment.”

Athleta’s net sales fell 14% year over year to $220 million, while comparable sales dropped 15%. Dickson acknowledged that efforts to modernize the brand’s assortment and marketing had fallen short amid growing competition.

“There’s new entrants reshaping the competitive landscape, and it is raising the bar for innovation, speed and relevance,” he said.

The company is now conducting a comprehensive review of Athleta, Dickson said.

Gap advances AI and digital engagement

Dickson said Gap Inc. remains the largest specialty apparel ecommerce business in the U.S. Its digital properties generated roughly 1.6 billion visits over the past 12 months, he said.

“We continue to advance our digital and app capabilities, including agentic commerce and, of course, always exploring emerging platforms like TikTok,” Dickson said.

Gap Inc. announced new AI shopping initiatives in October, including conversational product-discovery tools for Old Navy and Banana Republic. The retailer also partnered with Alta Daily to incorporate Gap merchandise into the styling app’s AI-generated outfit recommendations.

Gap is also using marketing partnerships to drive digital engagement.

Dickson said Old Navy’s back-to-school campaign with YouTube star MrBeast generated 1.4 billion global YouTube impressions, helping drive a more than 20% increase in traffic to its online children’s assortment. Dickson said Old Navy’s fall campaign with Cardi B also helped drive traffic while promoting its denim and cardigan assortments.

The company continues to update its physical footprint as well. Gap plans to remodel 35 Gap locations this year, bringing roughly a quarter of the brand’s North American specialty-store fleet into its latest format.

“The new Gap formats are outperforming their districts with really encouraging traffic and AUR (average unit retail) trends,” Dickson said.

Gap looks beyond apparel for growth

During Q3, Old Navy rolled out its beauty assortment nationwide. Dickson said customers purchasing beauty products are shopping across more of the store, with larger baskets and higher average transaction values than non-beauty shoppers.

The retailer is also seeing early momentum in accessories.

The Gap brand launched its first handbag collection in September. Dickson said several handbag styles sold out quickly, including the Five Pocket Tote, prompting the company to seek additional inventory.

Gap plans to introduce more handbag styles for the holiday season and expand its accessories offerings at Banana Republic and Old Navy in 2027. However, Dickson said they are not expected to make a meaningful financial contribution this year.

To further drive incremental sales, the company is also using licensing partnerships. Dickson said more than 60% of Old Navy shoppers who bought Fanatics merchandise also purchased products from the brand’s core apparel assortment, with baskets exceeding Old Navy’s average.

Gap lowers full-year outlook

Gap Inc. now expects fiscal 2026 revenue to be roughly flat year over year, down from its previous growth forecast of 1% to 1.5%.

Executives cited a slower-than-expected start to the holiday quarter. Old Navy increased promotions to attract shoppers, while Athleta stepped up discounting amid weaker sales.

Still, lower-than-expected U.S. tariff rates are projected to add roughly $46 million to Gap’s full-year operating profit, partially offsetting other pressures on the business. The retailer ended Q3 with $2.3 billion in inventory, down 6% from a year earlier.

Separately, Gap recorded a $420 million year-to-date adjustment to cost of goods sold related to the recovery of tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). It also recorded $21 million in related interest income. The company excluded both benefits from its adjusted full-year outlook.

Percentage changes may not align exactly with dollar figures due to rounding. Check back for more earnings reports. Here’s last quarter’s update on Gap revenue.
